warmup.q: A JVM is checkpointed after an hour of traffic, to be restored later on another machine of the same type. Its pool of 20 database connections is open at the moment of the checkpoint, and nobody wrote any CRaC hooks. What happens?
options: The restored JVM keeps using the 20 connections, because the image saved them
The checkpoint fails: with the default policy, open sockets stop it, and the process keeps running
The checkpoint succeeds, and the connections fail silently later
The JVM closes and reopens them by itself after the restore
warmup.why: CRaC's default policy for open files and sockets is error: print an error and fail the checkpoint. A connection also lives on the database server, which would have dropped its side long before the restore, so it couldn't be carried in an image anyway. The fix is a resource whose beforeCheckpoint closes the pool and whose afterRestore reconnects, as the third section shows.

opening:
One more picture from the shop. By mid-morning it's at its best: the shelves are full, the coffee machine is hot, and the shopkeeper knows where everything is. Imagine taking a photo of that moment and, the next day, stepping straight into it, shop and all, exactly as it was.

CRaC, Coordinated Restore at Checkpoint, does that for a running JVM. It saves the whole warm process to disk, and later starts copies from it that run at full speed from the first request. Lessons 1 to 3 got the program to its first request sooner, but none of them brought a warm JIT along.

The photo has one awkward limit: it can't hold the other end of a phone call. A connection to a database lives partly on another computer, which hung up long ago. Code that keeps one open makes the checkpoint fail. In this lesson, we'll watch a JVM warm up, take the photo, teach the tracking service's parts to let go first, and then choose among every tool in this track. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.
closing:
We started with a photo of the busy shop, and a phone call it can't hold. CRaC restores a warm JVM, compiled code and all, once every connection lets go and each copy gets fresh ids. That completes the toolbox: measure from outside, then pick an archive, a cache, a native image, a checkpoint or nothing.

Now note, for one of your services, how often it starts, who waits for it and what it holds open. Those answers choose the column.

That ends Part 4's tour of the JVM. Next, in the capstone, we'll build a tiny container that creates your objects and hands each one its helpers. How does it find your classes and call their constructors by reflection?

sections.h: A started JVM is still cold
sections.html:
Lessons 1 to 3 were about reaching the first request. There's a second wait after it. WarmupDemo, in the Try it below, starts a fresh JVM and runs the same work ten times: 20,000 check-digit tests on 16-digit tracking numbers. (A check digit is the last digit of a number, chosen so that a simple sum catches most typing mistakes.) On JDK 25.0.5, on a busy machine, one run printed:

round  1: 124,855 us
round  2:   6,307 us
round  3:   6,440 us
round  4:   5,474 us
round  5:   5,449 us
round  6:   4,710 us
round  7:   4,760 us
round  8:   4,635 us
round  9:   4,516 us
round 10:   5,141 us

Round 1 took 125 ms, and every round after it about 5 ms. Nothing in the code changed between rounds. The JVM did.

A fresh JVM runs every method in the interpreter, which executes bytecode one instruction at a time, and counts how often each method runs and each loop turns. When a method gets hot, C1, the JIT's quick compiler, compiles it with light optimization and keeps counting. When it stays hot, C2, the slow and thorough one, compiles it again using the profile: which branches were taken, and which classes arrived at each call. That climb is called warm-up, and every new JVM climbs it again. In the shop, it's the shopkeeper learning the popular items by heart, and forgetting them all every night.

The demo can switch parts of the climb off. With -Xint, the interpreter alone, every round took 164 to 323 ms and never got faster. With -XX:TieredStopAtLevel=1, C1 alone, round 1 took 28 ms and the rounds from 5 on about 5 ms.

That looks odd at first: C1 alone beat the default on round 1. In the default setup, C1's first versions also count branches and types for C2, which slows them down, and C2's own compiling competes for the machine's four busy cores, the processor's independent workers. The default pays early and catches up later. From round 6 on, both settled at about 4.5 to 5 ms, because a loop this simple gives C2 little to add.

The tools in this track each attack part of the wait. AppCDS and the AOT cache get classes ready sooner. On JDK 25, the AOT cache also hands the JIT the profiles from its training run (JEP 515), so it can start compiling sooner. The compiling still happens inside each new JVM, though; compiled code in the cache is JEP 544, still in development for JDK 28. A native image is compiled before it runs, so it never warms up, and it never reaches C2's profile-driven code either.

A JVM that has started isn't yet a JVM that's fast. Warm-up repeats in every new process.

Before the Try it, sketch the ten round times you expect with -Xint, and with C1 only.

CRaC takes a different route from all of them. It lets one JVM warm up, saves the whole running process to disk, and starts copies of it later, already warm.

try.title: Watch a JVM warm up
steps: Read WarmupDemo. It starts a fresh JVM and runs ten rounds of 20,000 check-digit tests on 16-digit tracking numbers, printing each round's time.
Run it as it is. Note round 1 and round 10.
Run it with -Pargs=-Xint, then with -Pargs=-XX:TieredStopAtLevel=1, after writing down your prediction for each.
Explain the three shapes with what the interpreter, C1 and C2 do.

code.title: WarmupDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.startup.l04.demo; import java.nio.file.Path; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.List; /** * Runs the same work in 10 rounds in a fresh JVM and prints how long each round took. A fresh * JVM starts in the interpreter, then the JIT compiles the hot code. Extra arguments are passed * to that JVM as flags, for example -Xint (interpreter only) or -XX:TieredStopAtLevel=1 (C1 only). */ public class WarmupDemo { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { if (args.length > 0 && args[0].equals("--work")) { work(); return; } List<String> cmd = new ArrayList<>(); cmd.add(Path.of(System.getProperty("java.home"), "bin", "java").toString()); cmd.addAll(List.of(args)); cmd.addAll(List.of("-cp", System.getProperty("java.class.path"), WarmupDemo.class.getName(), "--work")); System.out.println("fresh JVM, flags " + List.of(args)); Process child = new ProcessBuilder(cmd).redirectErrorStream(true).inheritIO().start(); child.waitFor(); } /** Ten rounds of 20,000 check-digit tests on 16-digit tracking numbers, the test every typed-in number gets. */ static void work() { long checksum = 0; for (int round = 1; round <= 10; round++) { long t0 = System.nanoTime(); for (int i = 0; i < 20_000; i++) { String digits = Long.toString(1_000_003L * i + round); String number = "7000" + "0".repeat(12 - digits.length()) + digits; // a 16-digit tracking number if (checkDigitOk(number)) checksum += i; } long us = (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000; System.out.printf("round %2d: %,7d us%n", round, us); } if (checksum == 42) System.out.println(); // keeps the JIT from dropping the work } /** The Luhn check: the last digit makes the weighted sum a multiple of 10, so most typos show. */ static boolean checkDigitOk(String number) { int sum = 0; boolean twice = false; for (int i = number.length() - 1; i >= 0; i--) { int d = number.charAt(i) - '0'; if (twice) { d *= 2; if (d > 9) d -= 9; } sum += d; twice = !twice; } return sum % 10 == 0; } }

alt.title: WarmupDemo.kt
alt.html: package workbench.startup.l04.demo import java.nio.file.Path /** * Runs the same work in 10 rounds in a fresh JVM and prints how long each round took. A fresh * JVM starts in the interpreter, then the JIT compiles the hot code. Extra arguments are passed * to that JVM as flags, for example -Xint (interpreter only) or -XX:TieredStopAtLevel=1 (C1 only). */ fun main(args: Array<String>) { if (args.firstOrNull() == "--work") { work() return } val cmd = listOf(Path.of(System.getProperty("java.home"), "bin", "java").toString()) + args + listOf("-cp", System.getProperty("java.class.path"), "workbench.startup.l04.demo.WarmupDemoKt", "--work") println("fresh JVM, flags ${args.toList()}") ProcessBuilder(cmd).redirectErrorStream(true).inheritIO().start().waitFor() } /** Ten rounds of 20,000 check-digit tests on 16-digit tracking numbers, the test every typed-in number gets. */ private fun work() { var checksum = 0L for (round in 1..10) { val t0 = System.nanoTime() for (i in 0 until 20_000) { val number = "7000" + (1_000_003L * i + round).toString().padStart(12, '0') // a 16-digit tracking number if (checkDigitOk(number)) checksum += i } val us = (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000 println("round %2d: %,7d us".format(round, us)) } if (checksum == 42L) println() // keeps the JIT from dropping the work } /** The Luhn check: the last digit makes the weighted sum a multiple of 10, so most typos show. */ private fun checkDigitOk(number: String): Boolean { var sum = 0 var twice = false for (i in number.indices.reversed()) { var d = number[i] - '0' if (twice) { d *= 2 if (d > 9) d -= 9 } sum += d twice = !twice } return sum % 10 == 0 }

try.expect: Three runs of each on JDK 25.0.5, on a busy machine: the default went from 75 to 128 ms in round 1 to about 3 to 7 ms from round 3 on, with an occasional spike to 10 or 30 ms when another program grabbed the cores. With -Xint every round took 150 to 360 ms and never got faster, because nothing is compiled. With C1 only, round 1 took 22 to 28 ms and later rounds about 5 ms: faster than the interpreter at once, and about as fast as C2 for a loop this simple. Your numbers will differ; the shapes won't.

sections.h: CRaC saves a warm JVM to disk and brings it back
sections.html:
CRaC stands for Coordinated Restore at Checkpoint. A checkpoint writes a running JVM to disk, and a restore starts a new process from that image. In the shop, the checkpoint is a photo of the busy shop, and the restore is stepping into that photo the next morning, with everything exactly as it was.

Under the hood, the OpenJDK implementation uses CRIU (Checkpoint/Restore In Userspace), a Linux tool that freezes a process. CRIU writes the process's memory pages, each thread's CPU registers (the processor's own small storage slots) and the state the operating system keeps for the process into a folder of image files. A restore builds a new process from those files, and the new process carries on at the instruction where the old one stopped. The heap, the loaded classes and the JIT's compiled code all come back as they were. The CRaC docs put it this way: "After the restore, Java runtime performance is also on-par with the one at the checkpoint."

The same mechanism tells you what can't come back. A network connection lives partly in the operating system and partly on the other computer, and the database at the other end dropped its side long before your restore. A file may have changed or moved. So the JVM tells your code before the checkpoint and after the restore, which is the "coordinated" part, and CRaC refuses to checkpoint while files or sockets are still open. (A socket is one end of a network connection, as your program sees it.)

The whole flow is three commands:

java -XX:CRaCCheckpointTo=cr -jar tracker.jar     # start; allows a checkpoint into the folder cr
jcmd tracker.jar JDK.checkpoint                   # after warm-up traffic: write the image, end the process
java -XX:CRaCRestoreFrom=cr                       # later, as often as you like: carry on from the image

There's one trap in those three lines, and jcmd is the cheerful culprit. The docs say "success is always reported in jcmd output, problems are reported in the console of the application". So jcmd prints "Command executed successfully" whatever happened, and only the application's own log tells you the truth.

The CRaC project published these "time to first operation" numbers in 2020. They come from an early CRaC build of JDK 14 on a laptop, for services written with three popular frameworks:

Service built with Normal start Restored
Spring Boot 3,898 ms 38 ms
Micronaut 1,001 ms 46 ms
Quarkus 980 ms 33 ms

Now the catch. CRaC isn't part of mainline OpenJDK: there's no JEP, and the main repository has no CRaC commits. You need a CRaC-enabled JDK build from a vendor. Azul ships CRaC in its Zulu builds of JDK 17, 21 and 25 for Linux on x64 and ARM64, in the files with "-crac-" in the name. BellSoft ships CRaC builds of Liberica JDK 17 and 21. CRIU needs extra rights from the operating system. Restoring on a computer with a different CPU can fail, unless you pin the CPU features with -XX:CPUFeatures when you take the checkpoint. And the image holds the whole heap, secrets included, so store it as carefully as a heap dump, a file of every object in memory.

Here the photo picture breaks, and the break matters. You can't step into the same photo twice, but you can restore one CRaC image into ten processes, and all ten wake up with exactly the same memory.

A checkpoint saves everything inside the process, and nothing outside it.

So before the checkpoint, everything that reaches outside the process has to let go, and after the restore it has to reach out again. Your code does that through two hooks.

try.title: Checkpoint and restore (optional, needs a CRaC JDK on Linux)
steps: If you have a CRaC-enabled JDK (for example a Zulu build with -crac- in its name), build any small service JAR and start it with the first command. Send it some requests.
Run the jcmd command. Look at both terminals: jcmd's and the application's.
Run the restore command and send a request at once. Compare how fast it answers with a normal start.
Without a CRaC JDK, answer this from the mechanism instead: your service opened a log file for appending and keeps it open. What does the checkpoint do, and why?

code.title: terminal (CRaC JDK on Linux)
code.html: java -XX:CRaCCheckpointTo=cr -jar tracker.jar # in a second terminal, after some traffic: jcmd tracker.jar JDK.checkpoint # later, as often as you like: java -XX:CRaCRestoreFrom=cr

try.expect: jcmd prints Command executed successfully whatever happened; the application's console shows any problem. If the checkpoint worked, the original process ends and cr is a folder of image files. The restore carries on from the checkpoint and answers like a warm JVM. The open log file fails the checkpoint under the default error policy, because an open file can't safely go into the image: the file might change or vanish before a restore.

video.title: A started JVM is still cold: CRaC saves a warm process to disk and restores it, once your resources let go

sections.h: Resources must let go before the checkpoint
sections.html:
Your code takes part through two methods. In the org.crac library (1.5.0 is the latest release), a resource, anything that must hear about checkpoints, looks like this:

Java
public final class DepotDbPool implements Resource {
    public DepotDbPool() {
        Core.getGlobalContext().register(this);    // the context only holds a weak reference
    }
    @Override public void beforeCheckpoint(Context<? extends Resource> c) { closeAllConnections(); }
    @Override public void afterRestore(Context<? extends Resource> c) { reconnect(); }
}
Kotlin
class DepotDbPool : Resource {
    init {
        Core.getGlobalContext().register(this)     // the context only holds a weak reference
    }
    override fun beforeCheckpoint(c: Context<out Resource>) = closeAllConnections()
    override fun afterRestore(c: Context<out Resource>) = reconnect()
}

The two versions match line for line; Kotlin writes Java's Context<? extends Resource> as Context<out Resource>. org.crac mirrors the jdk.crac API of CRaC JDKs, and finds the real implementation by reflection, looking it up by name, when the program runs. On a JDK without CRaC you can still register resources, and only a checkpoint request fails. So the same JAR runs everywhere.

The global context, the list of resources the JVM tells, follows documented rules. It calls beforeCheckpoint in the reverse order of registration, and afterRestore in registration order. Components created later usually use the earlier ones. The tracking service's scan listener, which reads scan messages from the depots, saves them through the database pool, so it must stop first and start last. In the shop, it's the closing routine: the last thing switched on in the morning is the first thing switched off at night.

Every resource is told, even when another one throws. The context collects the exceptions as suppressed exceptions on one CheckpointException. (A suppressed exception is an extra exception attached to the one that's thrown, so that none gets lost.) If the checkpoint fails, the restore notifications run at once, without an image, and the process carries on.

Open files and sockets fail the checkpoint by default. Their policy is error, which the CRaC docs describe as "just print error and fail the checkpoint". You can set other policies (ignore, close, reopen) in a file named by -Djdk.crac.resource-policies. For sockets, though, "the reopening part is not implemented, therefore will result in a runtime exception after restore". Close them yourself.

The image is one copy of memory, and every restore starts from it. Restore ten copies of the shop from one photo, and every till starts at ticket number 42. Anything generated before the checkpoint is the same in all ten: an instance id, a counter, a cached access token. Recreate those in afterRestore.

One more trap hides in that comment about weak references. The global context holds each resource weakly, so the garbage collector, the part of the JVM that frees unused memory, may remove a resource that nothing else refers to. Then its hooks never run. Keep the resource in a field of the component it belongs to, as the compare block below does.

Close what reaches outside before the checkpoint. Rebuild what must be unique after the restore.

That completes the toolbox. The last step is choosing from it.

try.title: Hook order, and a forgotten socket
steps: Read HookOrderDemo. Three components register in the order the tracking service creates them: the database pool, the scan listener, the stats reporter.
Predict the order of the six hook lines, then run it.
Run it with -Pargs=leak, where the reporter forgets to close its socket. Predict whether the restore hooks still run.

code.title: HookOrderDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.startup.l04.demo; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.List; /** * A toy checkpoint: three components register hooks in the order the service creates them. * Pass "leak" as an argument and the stats reporter forgets to close its socket. */ public class HookOrderDemo { /** org.crac.Resource has the same two methods, each taking a Context argument. */ interface Resource { void beforeCheckpoint(); void afterRestore(); } static final List<Resource> registered = new ArrayList<>(); static final List<String> openSockets = new ArrayList<>(); static final class Component implements Resource { final String name; final boolean leaks; Component(String name, boolean leaks) { this.name = name; this.leaks = leaks; openSockets.add(name); // every component holds a connection registered.add(this); // and registers itself when it is created } public void beforeCheckpoint() { System.out.println(" beforeCheckpoint: " + name); if (!leaks) openSockets.remove(name); } public void afterRestore() { System.out.println(" afterRestore: " + name); if (!openSockets.contains(name)) openSockets.add(name); } } public static void main(String[] args) { boolean leak = args.length > 0 && args[0].equals("leak"); new Component("database pool", false); // created first: the others use it new Component("scan listener", false); new Component("stats reporter", leak); System.out.println("checkpoint requested"); for (Resource r : registered.reversed()) r.beforeCheckpoint(); // last registered first if (openSockets.isEmpty()) { System.out.println(" -- snapshot written --"); } else { System.out.println(" -- checkpoint refused, still open: " + openSockets + " --"); } for (Resource r : registered) r.afterRestore(); // first registered first } }

alt.title: HookOrderDemo.kt
alt.html: package workbench.startup.l04.demo /** * A toy checkpoint: three components register hooks in the order the service creates them. * Pass "leak" as an argument and the stats reporter forgets to close its socket. */ private interface Hooks { // org.crac.Resource: the same two methods, plus a Context argument fun beforeCheckpoint() fun afterRestore() } private val registered = mutableListOf<Hooks>() private val openSockets = mutableListOf<String>() private class Component(val name: String, val leaks: Boolean) : Hooks { init { openSockets += name // every component holds a connection registered += this // and registers itself when it is created } override fun beforeCheckpoint() { println(" beforeCheckpoint: $name") if (!leaks) openSockets -= name } override fun afterRestore() { println(" afterRestore: $name") if (name !in openSockets) openSockets += name } } fun main(args: Array<String>) { val leak = args.firstOrNull() == "leak" Component("database pool", false) // created first: the others use it Component("scan listener", false) Component("stats reporter", leak) println("checkpoint requested") registered.asReversed().forEach { it.beforeCheckpoint() } // last registered first if (openSockets.isEmpty()) { println(" -- snapshot written --") } else { println(" -- checkpoint refused, still open: $openSockets --") } registered.forEach { it.afterRestore() } // first registered first }

try.expect: beforeCheckpoint runs for the stats reporter, the scan listener, then the database pool; then -- snapshot written --; then afterRestore runs for the pool, the listener, then the reporter. With leak, the checkpoint is refused (-- checkpoint refused, still open: [stats reporter] --), and the restore hooks still run in the same order, so the service keeps working. That's what the real global context does when a checkpoint fails.

aside.title: What is AWS Lambda SnapStart?
aside.html: AWS Lambda is a cloud service that runs your code only when a request arrives, starting new copies on demand. Its SnapStart feature takes a snapshot of an initialized Java function and restores it for each new copy, using the same org.crac hooks, and AWS documents the same hook order. It's a separate implementation, though: the Quarkus guide warns that "SnapStart is not CRaC and can do things that would not work with others CRaC implementations". Quarkus's SnapStart support also loads and initializes the classes listed in META-INF/quarkus-preload-classes.txt before the snapshot, which moves lesson 1's class loading into the image. Restoring has a time limit, so keep afterRestore short.

sections.html:
Here's the whole track in one table. The numbers come from the lessons: this track's own runs on a busy machine, the research behind the course, the Quarkus benchmark from lesson 3, and CRaC's 2020 results. Read them as directions, not promises.

Nothing AppCDS AOT cache Native image CRaC or SnapStart
In the shop unpack every morning yesterday's shelves in the back room the shelves, plus the notebook a pop-up stall from the factory a photo of the busy shop
Needs any JDK JDK 13+ for a dynamic archive JDK 24+; 25.0.4+ to be safe GraalVM or Mandrel a vendor CRaC JDK on Linux, or Lambda
Code changes none none none metadata, build-time initialization fixes hooks for sockets, files and pools
Start-up gain seen baseline about half the CPU about a sixth of the CPU; first request 218 to 136 ms first request 581 ms instead of 4,417 ms first operation 33 ms instead of 980 ms
Peak throughput baseline the same about 7% lower about 59% lower a warm JVM's
Memory (RSS) baseline a little lower 240 instead of 304 MiB 95 instead of 304 MiB a warm JVM's
What it costs nothing an archive step in the build a training run; the same JDK build, flags and JAR builds of 3 to 10 minutes and 4 to 8 GB CRIU rights, image storage, per-copy ids

Start with the JVM and measure, the way lesson 1 did: time to first request from outside, and RSS from ps. On JDK 25.0.4 or later, add the AOT cache, trained by your integration tests. It's the cheapest gain in the table, and it changes no code. On JDK 21, build a dynamic AppCDS archive when you build the program. For a service that rarely restarts and that nobody waits on, do nothing more.

Move to a native image when start-up in milliseconds, or memory per copy, is the real limit. Think of small tools people run from a terminal, functions that start on demand and stop when idle, or many small services packed onto one machine. The team must accept slow builds, metadata upkeep and lower peak throughput.

Move to CRaC or SnapStart when new copies must be fast and warm at once, and you control the runtime: Lambda, or a CRaC JDK on Linux with CRIU rights. You also need to make every connection pool, listener and open file checkpoint-safe.

Measure first. Then pick the cheapest column that meets the need.

Check yourself with a case the table doesn't list. A nightly batch job on JDK 25.0.5 runs for 40 minutes, starts once a night, and keeps the CPU busy the whole time. Which column wins? (Nothing, or at most the AOT cache. Its start-up is a rounding error next to 40 minutes, and a native image would cost it peak throughput in every minute of the run.)

compare.title: A checkpoint-safe pool with org.crac in Java and Kotlin

java.title: DepotClientPool.java
java.html: public final class DepotClientPool { private final List<DepotConnection> connections = new ArrayList<>(); // a field keeps the handler reachable: the global context only holds a weak reference private final Resource cracHandler = new Resource() { @Override public void beforeCheckpoint(Context<? extends Resource> c) { closeAll(); } @Override public void afterRestore(Context<? extends Resource> c) { openAll(); } }; public DepotClientPool() { openAll(); Core.getGlobalContext().register(cracHandler); } private synchronized void openAll() { for (int i = 0; i < 20; i++) connections.add(DepotConnection.open()); } private synchronized void closeAll() { connections.forEach(DepotConnection::close); // nothing open in the image connections.clear(); } }

kotlin.title: DepotClientPool.kt
kotlin.html: class DepotClientPool { private val connections = mutableListOf<DepotConnection>() // a property keeps the handler reachable: the global context only holds a weak reference private val cracHandler = object : Resource { override fun beforeCheckpoint(c: Context<out Resource>) = closeAll() override fun afterRestore(c: Context<out Resource>) = openAll() } // after cracHandler: Kotlin runs property initializers and init blocks top to bottom init { openAll() Core.getGlobalContext().register(cracHandler) } @Synchronized private fun openAll() = repeat(20) { connections += DepotConnection.open() } @Synchronized private fun closeAll() { connections.forEach { it.close() } // nothing open in the image connections.clear() } }

compare.note: The JVM sees the same thing from both: an object implementing org.crac.Resource, held strongly by the pool and weakly by the global context. Java's anonymous class and Kotlin's object : expression both compile to a small inner class, and Resource has two methods, so neither language can use a lambda for it. The Kotlin trap is order. Properties and init blocks run top to bottom. With the init block above cracHandler, a direct reference fails to compile ("variable 'cracHandler' must be initialized"), but the same reference made through a helper method compiles and registers null. Java runs all field initializers before the constructor body, so the Java version has no such trap. Kotlin also writes the parameter as Context<out Resource>, which is Java's Context<? extends Resource>.

steps.say: List what the tracking service holds that lives outside the process. There's a database pool, and a scan listener that reads messages from a message queue (a server that holds messages until a reader takes them) and saves them through the pool. There's also an instance id that starts every event id the service writes. The pool and the listener hold sockets. The instance id is plain memory, and that's its problem: every restored copy would get the same one.

Give the listener its hooks. It's created after the pool, so it's registered later, which makes the context stop it before the pool closes and start it after the pool is back. Keep the handler in a field.
steps.code: final class ScanListener { private volatile QueueReader reader = newReader(); private final Resource cracHandler = new Resource() { // 1. stop reading, finish the message in hand, and close the queue connection @Override public void beforeCheckpoint(Context<? extends Resource> c) { stopReading(); reader.close(); } // 2. a new reader connects again after the restore @Override public void afterRestore(Context<? extends Resource> c) { reader = newReader(); startReading(); } }; ScanListener() { Core.getGlobalContext().register(cracHandler); } }

alt.html: class ScanListener { @Volatile private var reader = newReader() private val cracHandler = object : Resource { // 1. stop reading, finish the message in hand, and close the queue connection override fun beforeCheckpoint(c: Context<out Resource>) { stopReading(); reader.close() } // 2. a new reader connects again after the restore override fun afterRestore(c: Context<out Resource>) { reader = newReader(); startReading() } } init { Core.getGlobalContext().register(cracHandler) } }

steps.say: Make per-copy state after the restore. The instance id moves out of a final field and into something afterRestore can replace, so two copies restored from one image never write the same event id.
steps.code: final class InstanceId implements Resource { private volatile String value = UUID.randomUUID().toString(); InstanceId() { Core.getGlobalContext().register(this); } // kept alive by whoever holds InstanceId String get() { return value; } @Override public void beforeCheckpoint(Context<? extends Resource> c) { } // 3. every restored copy gets its own id @Override public void afterRestore(Context<? extends Resource> c) { value = UUID.randomUUID().toString(); } }

alt.html: class InstanceId : Resource { @Volatile var value: String = UUID.randomUUID().toString() private set init { Core.getGlobalContext().register(this) } // kept alive by whoever holds InstanceId override fun beforeCheckpoint(c: Context<out Resource>) {} // 3. every restored copy gets its own id override fun afterRestore(c: Context<out Resource>) { value = UUID.randomUUID().toString() } }

steps.say: Test the checkpoint for real on a CRaC JDK, and read the application's console, because jcmd reports success either way. A refused checkpoint names what was still open.
steps.code: java -XX:CRaCCheckpointTo=cr -jar tracker.jar & # send some traffic, then: jcmd tracker.jar JDK.checkpoint # prints "Command executed successfully" in any case # check the service's own log for errors, then restore and track a parcel: java -XX:CRaCRestoreFrom=cr

lab.title: Build a checkpoint context and a checkpoint-safe pool
steps: Run the tests once. Seven of the eight fail; borrow already works.

Implement SimContext.checkpointRestore, a simulated global context, following the four numbered rules in its KDoc. They are the rules the org.crac docs give for the real one. Run SimContextTest until its four tests pass.

Fix DepotConnectionPool, the tracking service's pool of database connections: register it with the context in init, close and drop every socket in beforeCheckpoint, and open size new ones in afterRestore.
Run all eight tests. Then read after restore the pool hands out new, open connections: the socket ids prove the pool reconnected instead of reusing the old sockets.
hints: resources.asReversed() gives a reversed view of the list without copying it.
Collect problems in a mutableListOf<Exception>(), then CheckpointException("checkpoint failed").apply { problems.forEach(::addSuppressed) }.
When the checkpoint fails, restore notifications still run on every resource, and their exceptions go into the same CheckpointException.
lab.done: All eight tests in SimContextTest and DepotConnectionPoolTest pass.

drill.title: Hooks for a stats reporter, from memory
drill.prompt: Close this page. A StatsReporter sends counters over a socket every 10 seconds from a ScheduledExecutorService. Write its org.crac hooks: before the checkpoint, stop the schedule and close the socket; after the restore, open a new socket and schedule again. Keep the handler reachable, and register it.

answer.html: public final class StatsReporter { private ScheduledExecutorService timer; private StatsSocket socket; // held in a field: the global context only keeps a weak reference private final Resource cracHandler = new Resource() { @Override public void beforeCheckpoint(Context<? extends Resource> c) throws Exception { timer.shutdownNow(); // 1. no thread sends during the checkpoint timer.awaitTermination(5, TimeUnit.SECONDS); socket.close(); // 2. nothing open in the image } @Override public void afterRestore(Context<? extends Resource> c) { start(); // 3. a new socket and a new schedule } }; public StatsReporter() { start(); Core.getGlobalContext().register(cracHandler); } private void start() { socket = StatsSocket.connect("stats.internal:8125"); timer = Executors.newSingleThreadScheduledExecutor(); timer.scheduleAtFixedRate(this::send, 10, 10, TimeUnit.SECONDS); } private void send() { socket.write(Counters.snapshot()); } }

alt.html: class StatsReporter { private lateinit var timer: ScheduledExecutorService private lateinit var socket: StatsSocket // held in a property: the global context only keeps a weak reference private val cracHandler = object : Resource { override fun beforeCheckpoint(c: Context<out Resource>) { timer.shutdownNow() // 1. no thread sends during the checkpoint timer.awaitTermination(5, TimeUnit.SECONDS) socket.close() // 2. nothing open in the image } override fun afterRestore(c: Context<out Resource>) = start() // 3. new socket, new schedule } init { // after cracHandler, so it is set start() Core.getGlobalContext().register(cracHandler) } private fun start() { socket = StatsSocket.connect("stats.internal:8125") timer = Executors.newSingleThreadScheduledExecutor() timer.scheduleAtFixedRate({ socket.write(Counters.snapshot()) }, 10, 10, TimeUnit.SECONDS) } }

recap: A started JVM is still cold: it interprets, then C1 compiles, then C2 recompiles hot code with profiles. Every new JVM warms up again.

CRaC checkpoints a running JVM to disk with CRIU and restores it later, with heap, classes and compiled code as they were. It isn't in mainline OpenJDK: you need a CRaC-enabled vendor build on Linux, such as Azul Zulu (17, 21, 25) or BellSoft Liberica (17, 21).

Open files and sockets fail the checkpoint by default (the error policy). Close them in beforeCheckpoint, reopen them in afterRestore, and recreate per-copy state, because every restore starts from the same memory.

The global context calls beforeCheckpoint in reverse registration order and afterRestore in registration order, tells every resource even when one throws, and holds resources by weak reference, so keep yours in a field.

Default to the JVM plus the AOT cache (JDK 25.0.4+) or AppCDS (JDK 21). Go native when start-up or memory per copy is the real limit; use CRaC or SnapStart when copies must start fast and warm and you control the runtime.
The limit: each tool trades something. A cache is tied to one build, a native image to one closed world, and a checkpoint to one moment in memory. None of them replaces measuring from outside.

explain.prompt: A teammate asks: "If CRaC restores in 30 milliseconds, why don't we use it for every service instead of the AOT cache?" Answer them in your own words.
explain.answer: CRaC is fast because it restores the whole process memory, compiled code included, and that same mechanism is what makes it costly. Anything outside the process can't be in the image, so every pool, listener, client and open file needs hooks that close it before the checkpoint and reopen it after, in the right order, or the checkpoint fails. Every restored copy shares the image's memory, so per-copy ids and tokens must be made again. It also needs a vendor CRaC JDK on Linux with CRIU rights, or Lambda, and somewhere safe to keep images, which contain the heap with its secrets. The AOT cache needs no code changes and no special JDK beyond 25.0.4 or later, and it's simply ignored when it doesn't match. So I'd start with the AOT cache everywhere, and use CRaC only where a warm copy at once is worth that work.

deeper.html:
Three details for when you try CRaC for real.

First, the threads. A resource can be called while other threads still use the component. The CRaC best-practices guide sorts components by how threads reach them: an unknown number of threads arriving at random, a known number of threads arriving now and then, or an event loop. For the first case it suggests a java.util.concurrent.locks.ReadWriteLock: borrowers take the read lock, and beforeCheckpoint takes the write lock and keeps it until afterRestore, so callers wait during the checkpoint instead of failing on a closed connection.

Second, the policies. If a library holds a file you can't close, -Djdk.crac.resource-policies=<file> points at a policy file. Rules are separated by ---, match by type (file, pipe, socket, filedescriptor) and by fields such as the path or port, and the first matching rule wins. ignore leaves the descriptor to CRIU, close closes it ("an attempt to use it after restore will fail"), and reopen reopens a file at the same position. Use policies as a stopgap; hooks in your own code are clearer.

Third, the warm-up you capture. The CRaC docs describe the intended flow as a canary deployment: a new version first serves a little real traffic, which triggers class loading and JIT compilation, then you checkpoint it, and the image becomes part of the release. A checkpoint taken after a made-up warm-up only contains what that warm-up exercised, the same lesson as lesson 2's training run. For Lambda, the Quarkus SnapStart guide also suggests -XX:+TieredCompilation -XX:TieredStopAtLevel=1 through JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS, which trades peak speed for less compiling right after a restore. The C1-only run in this lesson's first Try it shows that trade.
